The Common goby Pomatoschistus microps exhibits a life-history strategy finely tuned to the variable thermal regimes of intertidal and estuarine environments across northwestern Europe. At a water temperature of 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C], a predictable pattern of early development unfolds, with yolk-sac larvae emerging from the demersal eggs after approximately 8.5 days [ab = approximately 8.5 days]. These lecithotrophic larvae, measuring around 0.00205 grams [Wwb = around 0.00205 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture, rely entirely on endogenous reserves during the initial post-hatching phase. The onset of exogenous feeding typically coincides with complete yolk absorption, marking a critical transition for the newly hatched prolarvae. The timing of these early life events is strongly mediated by temperature, with warmer conditions accelerating developmental rates and cooler conditions extending the yolk-dependent period.

Sexual maturation in Pomatoschistus microps is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, a pattern commonly seen in small-bodied gobiids. Females typically attain puberty once they reach a total length of 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet body mass of approximately 0.23 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.23 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from local populations. This size at maturity is relatively modest compared to congeneric species such as Pomatoschistus minutus, which often delay reproduction until a larger body size is achieved. The onset of reproductive activity is triggered by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Individuals that reach this size early in the growing season are able to contribute to the first spawning pulse of the year.

Reproductive output in the Common goby is characterized by a high frequency of spawning events within a single breeding season. Females produce multiple clutches over the course of several months, with each clutch containing a modest number of eggs. The maximum recorded reproductive output, observed under controlled laboratory conditions at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], is approximately 4.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 4.5 eggs per clutch] with females spawning at a frequency of roughly 1 clutch every 3 days [F_R_i = roughly 1 clutch every 3 days] over the peak spawning period when food availability is high. This figure reflects a combination of moderate clutch sizes and short inter-spawning intervals, typical of a multiple-batch spawner. The eggs themselves are adhesive and demersal, deposited on hard substrates or within empty bivalve shells where the male guards them until hatching.

Female Common gobies exhibit determinate growth patterns, reaching their ultimate size after the first one to two years of life. The maximum recorded total length for females, 9 cm [Li = 9 cm], corresponds to an asymptotic wet body mass of 6.74 grams [Wwi = 6.74 grams] as derived from allometric equations based on field-collected specimens. This ultimate body size is achieved gradually over successive growing seasons, with the most rapid linear growth occurring during the first year post-settlement. The size spectrum of mature females ranges widely, from newly pubertal individuals at 3 cm to large, gravid females approaching the asymptotic length. Body condition and lipid reserves are known to influence both fecundity per spawning event and the frequency of successive spawnings throughout the summer.

Longevity records for the Common goby indicate a relatively short life span typical of small, fast-lived Gobiiformes. At a mean annual water temperature of 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C], the oldest documented individuals survive for approximately 949 days [am = approximately 949 days], although most adults likely die after their first reproductive season due to the high energetic costs of repeated spawning. This maximum lifespan is comparable to that reported for other temperate Pomatoschistus species, though populations inhabiting colder, more stable thermal regimes may experience slightly extended longevity. The post-reproductive period, if it exists at all, is brief; senescence proceeds rapidly once the final clutch is deposited and the male's guarding duties conclude. Population turnover is therefore high, and the species relies heavily on annual recruitment from the previous year's spawning cohort to maintain local abundance.
